title: Diaphragm and its parts

objective.text: Trace how each part of the diaphragm arises and how it reaches its adult level.

body.general: Why is your breathing muscle's nerve a neck nerve? Early on, two channels beside the gut, the pericardioperitoneal canals, link the chest and belly [f1]. They lie beside a plate, the septum transversum [f1]. From week 5 a pleuroperitoneal fold grows from each channel wall [f2]. By week 7 the folds are thin sheets, the pleuroperitoneal membranes, that seal the channels [f3]. These make the tough centre, the central tendon [f4]. Muscle comes from somites, tissue blocks at neck levels C3–C5 [f5]. So the diaphragm's phrenic nerve is a neck nerve, lengthened as the diaphragm sinks [f7,f8].
body.mbbs: The septum transversum leaves two pericardioperitoneal canals beside the foregut, so chest and belly still connect [f1]. From the start of week 5, crescent pleuroperitoneal folds grow from the canal walls [f2]. By week 7 they are pleuroperitoneal membranes that fuse with the oesophageal mesentery and the septum transversum, closing the canals [f3]. In Langman 14e the fused membranes make the central tendon [f4]. Their rim is connective tissue that guides incoming muscle cells [f4]. Muscle comes from C3–C5 somites [f5]. The oesophageal mesentery forms the crura [f6]. The phrenic nerve is C3–C5 because the diaphragm starts opposite these segments in week 4 [f7]. From week 6 the back outgrows the front, moving the diaphragm caudally and lengthening the phrenic nerves [f8].

facts.text: The septum transversum leaves two pericardioperitoneal canals beside the foregut, so the chest and belly cavities still connect.
From the start of week 5, crescent-shaped pleuroperitoneal folds grow from the walls of the canals.
By week 7 the folds are thin pleuroperitoneal membranes that fuse with the oesophageal mesentery and the septum transversum, closing the canals.
facts.note: timing consistent with R05ai: the diaphragm cuts off the infracardiac bursa by CS17–18 (42–48 d)

facts.text: The fused pleuroperitoneal membranes make the central tendon; their rim is connective tissue that guides incoming muscle cells.
facts.note: R05aa: mouse lineage tracing, full text; D-043 (c)

facts.text: Diaphragm muscle comes from somites at the C3–C5 neck levels.
The oesophageal mesentery forms the crura of the diaphragm.
The phrenic nerve (motor and sensory) comes from C3–C5 because the diaphragm starts opposite these neck segments in week 4.
From week 6 the back outgrows the front, so the diaphragm moves ventrally and caudally to its adult level and the phrenic nerves lengthen.
In congenital diaphragmatic hernia, muscle usually fails to fill part of a pleuroperitoneal membrane because its connective-tissue scaffold fails.
facts.note: mouse: Gata4 loss in fold-derived fibroblasts gives muscle-free weak patches and hernias

facts.text: Most severe diaphragmatic hernias, about 85–90 %, are on the left.
Organs pushed into the chest keep the lungs small (lung hypoplasia), which is often fatal.
Beyond Langman (human study): the last part of each canal to close lies behind the adrenal gland; fold tissue seals it by spreading sideways.
facts.note: human, CRL 11–40 mm; depth on how the last dorsolateral part closes (G-Sci round 1)

facts.text: Beyond Langman (mouse study): fold cells spread over the liver surface ahead of the muscle, and muscle cells follow them.

misconceptions.wrong: The septum transversum forms the central tendon (the 'four parts' list in many books).
misconceptions.right: In Langman 14e the fused pleuroperitoneal membranes make the central tendon; the septum transversum is the base they grow over.

misconceptions.wrong: The diaphragm forms where it ends up.
misconceptions.right: It starts opposite C3–C5 and moves down, which is why the phrenic nerve is a long neck nerve.

misconceptions.wrong: Diaphragm muscle comes from the septum transversum.
misconceptions.right: It comes from somites at C3–C5.

checks.prompt: In Langman 14e, what makes the central tendon of the diaphragm?
checks.why: The pleuroperitoneal membranes fuse into the central tendon over the septum transversum, their base; somites give the muscle.

checks.prompt: Why is the phrenic nerve from C3–C5?
options: The diaphragm starts opposite those neck segments, then moves down
Its muscle comes from the septum transversum
Neck nerves grow down to find the finished diaphragm
The lungs drag the nerve down from the neck
checks.why: The diaphragm begins at neck level in week 4 and descends as the back outgrows the front, taking its C3–C5 nerve with it.

options: Two canals beside the gut link the chest and belly
Pleuroperitoneal folds grow out on each side
Pleuroperitoneal membranes seal off the canals
The diaphragm sinks to its adult level
checks.why: Week 5 folds become week 7 membranes that seal the canals; only then is the diaphragm finished at its adult level, its rim filled with C3–C5 muscle.

adult: The adult diaphragm: central tendon from the membranes, muscle from C3–C5 somites, phrenic nerve from C3–C5 [f4,f5,f7].
clinical: If muscle fails to fill part of a pleuroperitoneal membrane, belly organs can slip into the chest: congenital diaphragmatic hernia [f9,f11]. Most severe ones are on the left [f10]. The danger is small lungs, squeezed by the organs in the chest [f11].

remember.q: What makes the central tendon in Langman 14e?
Where does the diaphragm's muscle come from?
remember.a: From somites, tissue blocks at the C3–C5 neck levels [f5].

remember.q: Why is the phrenic nerve a long neck nerve?
remember.a: The diaphragm starts opposite C3–C5 in week 4, then moves down as the back outgrows the front [f7,f8].

remember.q: What links the chest and belly cavities before the diaphragm closes?
remember.a: Two pericardioperitoneal canals beside the gut [f1].
